title: Variables, Types & Zero Values
summary: Go is statically typed: every variable has a type fixed at compile time. You declare variables with `var` or the short form `:=`, and crucially, a variable with no explicit value is never garbage — it gets its type's **zero value** (0, "", false, or nil). This guarantee eliminates a whole class of uninitialized-memory bugs.

subtopics.title: Declaring with var
subtopics.explanation: `var name type` declares a variable; you can add an initializer, and with one the type may be omitted and is inferred. `var` works at both package and function scope, which makes it the only choice for package-level declarations. It is the foundational way to introduce a typed variable and, when written without an initializer, cleanly demonstrates the zero-value guarantee central to Variables, Types & Zero Values.
subtopics.example:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var count int    // no initializer -> zero value
	var name = "Ada" // type inferred from initializer
	var active bool  // zero value false
	fmt.Println(count, name, active) // Output: 0 Ada false
}

subtopics.title: Short declaration :=
subtopics.explanation: Inside functions, `name := value` declares and initializes in one step, inferring the type from the value. It can't be used at package scope and can't omit the value, but it's the most common form you'll write day to day. As a concise variable declaration it ties directly into Variables, Types & Zero Values by letting the compiler pick the type while you focus on the value.
subtopics.example:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x := 42            // inferred int
	s := "hi"          // inferred string
	pi := 3.14         // inferred float64
	ok := true         // inferred bool
	fmt.Println(x, s, pi, ok) // Output: 42 hi 3.14 true
}

subtopics.title: Type inference
subtopics.explanation: When you initialize a variable without stating its type, Go infers it from the value's default type: integer literals become `int`, decimals become `float64`, quoted text becomes `string`. Both `var x = ...` and `x := ...` rely on this. Inference is a core mechanic of Variables, Types & Zero Values because every variable still ends up with one fixed, statically known type even when you never spell it out.
subtopics.example:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	i := 42          // int
	f := 3.14        // float64
	s := "go"        // string
	b := true        // bool
	fmt.Printf("%T %T %T %T\n", i, f, s, b) // Output: int float64 string bool
}

subtopics.title: Zero values
subtopics.explanation: A declared-but-uninitialized variable holds its type's zero value: 0 for numbers, false for bool, "" for string, and nil for pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, and interfaces. There is no 'undefined' state in Go. This guarantee is the heart of Variables, Types & Zero Values, ensuring every variable is safe to read the instant it is declared.
subtopics.example:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var n int    // 0
	var f float64 // 0
	var s string // ""
	var b bool   // false
	var p *int   // nil
	fmt.Printf("%d %g %q %t %v\n", n, f, s, b, p) // Output: 0 0 "" false <nil>
}

subtopics.title: Basic types
subtopics.explanation: Go has sized integers (int, int8..int64, uint...), floats (float32, float64), bool, string, plus the aliases byte (uint8) and rune (int32 for Unicode code points). `int` is 64-bit on modern platforms. Knowing these building blocks is essential to Variables, Types & Zero Values because each type determines both the values a variable can hold and its zero value.
subtopics.example:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var b byte = 65    // uint8 alias
	var r rune = '世'   // int32 Unicode code point
	var f float64 = 2.5
	var ok bool = true
	fmt.Println(b, r, f, ok)        // Output: 65 19990 2.5 true
	fmt.Println(string(b), string(r)) // Output: A 世
}

subtopics.title: Explicit type conversion
subtopics.explanation: Go has no implicit numeric conversions — mixing types like int and float64 is a compile error. You must convert explicitly with T(x), which produces a new value of type T. This strictness prevents silent precision loss and surprising coercions, and it reinforces Variables, Types & Zero Values by keeping each variable's type explicit and intentional.

subtopics.title: Constants vs variables
subtopics.explanation: Variables can change at run time; constants (declared with const) are fixed at compile time. Untyped constants like 42 adapt to the context they're used in, which is why x := 42 becomes int but var f float64 = 42 becomes a float. Distinguishing the two rounds out Variables, Types & Zero Values by clarifying which typed storage can be reassigned and which cannot.
subtopics.example:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	const Pi = 3.14159 // untyped constant, fixed at compile time
	radius := 2.0      // variable, can change
	radius = 3.0
	fmt.Println(Pi * radius * radius) // Output: 28.27431
}

foundations.overview: In Go, every variable has a single, fixed type known when the program compiles — you can't put a string into an int variable later. You declare variables either with the explicit `var` keyword or the concise `:=` short form inside functions. The defining Go feature here is zero values: if you declare a variable without giving it a value, Go doesn't leave it pointing at random memory — it initializes it to a well-defined zero (0, false, "", or nil depending on the type). This makes Go code predictable and removes the uninitialized-variable bugs common in C.
foundations.formalDefinition: A variable is a typed, named storage location. Go is statically and strongly typed: types are checked at compile time and not implicitly converted. Any variable declared without an explicit initializer is set to the zero value of its type.
foundations.whyItMatters: Variables and types are the bedrock of every program. Go's zero-value guarantee and lack of implicit conversions shape how you write safe, idiomatic code, and questions about zero values and type conversions are extremely common in interviews.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of each variable as a labeled, pre-formatted box sized for exactly one type. If you don't put anything in it, it isn't empty in a dangerous way — it comes with a sensible default already inside (0, "", false, or nil).
commonUseCases: Counters and accumulators starting at zero
Structs designed to be usable at their zero value
Using nil as the 'not present' value for pointers/maps

commonMisconceptions.myth: An unassigned variable is undefined or random.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's the type's zero value — 0, false, "", or nil — always well-defined.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Go converts between number types automatically.
commonMisconceptions.reality: There are no implicit conversions; you must write float64(i) or int(f) explicitly.
Short declaration only works inside functions and requires an initializer; package-level declarations use var.

visualExplorer.title: Declaring a variable and its zero value
visualExplorer.caption: What the compiler does when you declare a variable.

config.intro: From declaration to a usable, zeroed variable:

steps.name: Determine the type
steps.detail: Either you state it (var x int) or the compiler infers it from the initializer (x := 42 -> int).

steps.name: Allocate storage
steps.detail: The compiler reserves memory sized for that exact type.

steps.name: Apply the zero value
steps.detail: If there's no initializer, the storage is set to the type's zero: 0, false, "", or nil.

steps.name: Or store the initializer
steps.detail: If you gave a value, it's stored, after any explicit conversion you wrote (Go never converts implicitly).

steps.name: Use it safely
steps.detail: Because there's no uninitialized state, reading the variable always yields a defined value.

interactiveExamples.title: Zero values of the basic types
interactiveExamples.explanation: Each variable is declared with var and no initializer, so each holds its type's zero value. The %q verb quotes the string so the empty string is visible.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: fix the type mismatch
interactiveExamples.explanation: Go won't add an int and a float64 directly — that's a compile error. Convert one explicitly so the types match, then print the sum.

code.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	i := 3                       // int
	f := 2.5                     // float64
	sum := float64(i) + f        // explicit conversion required
	fmt.Println(sum)             // 5.5
}

checkpoints.explanation: The zero value of a string is the empty string (printed as "" by %q) and the zero value of an int is 0. Strings are never nil — that's only for pointers, slices, maps, etc.

checkpoints.explanation: Go has no implicit numeric conversion. int and float64 can't be multiplied directly; write float64(x) * y. This strictness prevents silent precision bugs.

checkpoints.prompt: Which declaration is INVALID at package scope (outside any function)?
checkpoints.explanation: The short form := only works inside functions. At package scope you must use var (with or without an explicit type/initializer).

checkpoints.code:
var b byte = 65
var r rune = 'A'
fmt.Println(b, r)
checkpoints.explanation: byte (uint8) and rune (int32) are integer types, so Println shows their numeric values. 'A' is the code point 65. To print the character, convert to string: string(r).

codeLab.title: Summarize with a zero-value-friendly type
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Average(nums []int) float64` returning the mean of nums, or 0 when nums is empty. Lean on int's zero value (0) for the running sum and handle the empty case cleanly.
hints: Accumulate into an int sum starting at its zero value.
Convert both sum and len to float64 explicitly before dividing.

debuggingLab.title: The average is wrong (integer division)
debuggingLab.symptom: Average of 1 and 2 prints 1 instead of 1.5.

brokenCode.code:
a, b := 1, 2
avg := (a + b) / 2     // both ints -> integer division
fmt.Println(float64(avg)) // converts AFTER truncation

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Because a and b are ints, (a+b)/2 is integer division: 3/2 = 1, dropping the fraction. Converting to float64 afterward is too late — the precision is already gone. You must convert before dividing.
commonMistakes: Dividing ints then converting, instead of converting then dividing.
Assuming Go promotes ints to floats automatically in division.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Convert to float64 before the division so the fractional part survives.

solution.code:
a, b := 1, 2
avg := float64(a+b) / 2.0  // convert first, then divide
fmt.Println(avg)           // 1.5

theory.question: What are zero values in Go and why do they matter?
theory.directAnswer: A zero value is the default a variable gets when declared without an explicit initializer: 0 for numeric types, false for bool, "" for string, and nil for pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, and interfaces. They matter because they guarantee every variable starts in a well-defined state — Go has no uninitialized/undefined memory — which removes a whole class of bugs.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The default value of each type, applied automatically on declaration.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To make programs predictable and safe by eliminating uninitialized memory.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Allocation zeroes the storage; the type determines what 'zero' means.

theory.whyImportant: Designing types whose zero value is useful is idiomatic Go and a common interview theme.
theory.realWorldExample: A sync.Mutex and bytes.Buffer are usable immediately at their zero value — no constructor needed.

followUps.question: What's the zero value of a slice?
followUps.answer: nil — a nil slice has len 0 and cap 0 but you can still append to and range over it.

followUps.question: Is a string ever nil?
followUps.answer: No — strings are value types; their zero value is the empty string "".

theory.question: Why does Go require explicit type conversions, and when do you need them?
theory.directAnswer: Go is strongly typed and performs no implicit numeric conversions, so mixing types (like int and float64) in an expression is a compile error. You convert explicitly with T(x) — e.g. float64(i) or int(f) — whenever types differ. This prevents silent precision loss and surprising coercions.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Mandatory, explicit conversions between distinct types.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To make data-type changes visible and intentional, avoiding hidden bugs.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The conversion T(x) produces a new value of type T from x; the compiler enforces it where types differ.

theory.whyImportant: Integer-division and type-mismatch bugs are common; explicit conversion is the fix.
theory.realWorldExample: Computing a ratio: float64(hits) / float64(total) to avoid integer division.

followUps.question: Does := perform conversion?
followUps.answer: No — := only infers the type of the initializer; it never converts between types.

theory.question: What is the difference between declaring a variable with var and with the short form :=, and where can each be used?
theory.directAnswer: var name type [= value] declares a variable and works at both package and function scope; the type may be omitted when there's an initializer, and with no initializer the variable gets its zero value. The short form name := value works only inside functions, always requires an initializer, and infers the type from the value. So package-level declarations must use var, while inside functions := is the common, concise choice.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two syntaxes for introducing a typed variable in Go.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: var covers all scopes and the zero-value case; := gives brevity for the common in-function initialized case.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler infers the type from the initializer for := and for var without a stated type; var alone applies the zero value.

theory.whyImportant: Using := at package scope is a common beginner compile error; knowing the boundary avoids it.
theory.realWorldExample: A package-level config default uses var Timeout = 30, while a loop counter inside a function uses i := 0.

followUps.question: Can you declare without initializing using :=?
followUps.answer: No — := always requires a value; use var name type when you want the zero value.

followUps.question: Can := redeclare an existing variable?
followUps.answer: It can reuse a name in a multi-assignment as long as at least one variable on the left is new.

theory.question: What are byte and rune in Go, and how do they differ?
theory.directAnswer: byte is an alias for uint8 and represents a single raw byte, while rune is an alias for int32 and represents a Unicode code point. Both are integer types, so printing them shows numbers unless you convert to string. Use byte for raw/ASCII bytes and rune when you need to handle full Unicode characters correctly.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two named aliases for integer types used for text handling.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To express intent — raw bytes vs. Unicode code points — while staying integer types.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: byte == uint8 (0-255); rune == int32 holding a code point; ranging over a string yields runes, indexing yields bytes.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing bytes and runes causes garbled multi-byte (e.g. non-ASCII) text handling.
theory.realWorldExample: Iterating a string with range gives runes so '世' is one code point, not several bytes.

followUps.question: What does len("世") return?
followUps.answer: 3 — len counts bytes, and that character is 3 bytes in UTF-8; the rune count is 1.

scenario.question: You design a Config struct. How can zero values make its API simpler, and what's the risk?
scenario.directAnswer: Design fields so the zero value is a sensible default — then callers can use Config{} directly and only set what they need. The risk is ambiguity: for some fields 0 or "" is a legitimate value AND the 'unset' signal, so you can't tell them apart. Use a pointer (*int) or a bool 'set' flag when you must distinguish 'unset' from a real zero.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Leveraging zero values for default-friendly struct APIs.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go idiom 'make the zero value useful' reduces boilerplate constructors.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Unset struct fields are already zeroed; only override what differs.

scenario.whyImportant: Good zero-value design is a hallmark of idiomatic Go APIs.
scenario.realWorldExample: http.Server{} works with sensible defaults; you set only Addr and Handler.

followUps.question: How do you tell 'unset' from a real 0?
followUps.answer: Use a pointer field (*int): nil means unset, &0 means an explicit zero.

scenario.question: A colleague's rate calculation divides two int counters and always gets 0 or a rounded value. What's the bug and how do you fix it idiomatically?
scenario.directAnswer: int/int does integer division in Go, truncating the fraction — 3/4 is 0, not 0.75. Because Go performs no implicit conversions, converting after dividing is too late. Convert the operands to float64 before dividing: float64(hits) / float64(total). Guard total == 0 first to avoid a divide-by-zero panic.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An integer-division precision bug rooted in Go's strict typing.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go never implicitly promotes ints to floats, so arithmetic stays in the operands' type.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Explicit float64(x) conversions make the division floating-point, preserving the fraction.

scenario.whyImportant: Integer division is one of the most common numeric bugs for newcomers to Go.
scenario.realWorldExample: A cache hit-rate metric returns 0.0 until both counters are converted to float64 before dividing.

followUps.question: Where should the conversion happen?
followUps.answer: Before the division — float64(a)/float64(b) — not after, since truncation already lost the fraction.

followUps.question: What about dividing by zero?
followUps.answer: Integer divide-by-zero panics; float divide-by-zero yields +Inf/NaN, so guard total==0 explicitly.

systemDesign.question: You are designing configuration structs for a service. How can you exploit Go's zero-value guarantee to make a clean, usable-by-default API, and when must you deviate?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Design each field so its zero value is the sensible default, so callers can write Config{} and override only what differs — the idiomatic 'make the zero value useful' approach. Deviate when 0, "", or false is both a legitimate value and the 'unset' signal; then use a pointer field (*int) or an explicit 'set' bool so you can distinguish an intentional zero from an unspecified one.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Applying Go's zero-value semantics to configuration and constructor design.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because every field is auto-zeroed, defaults can be implicit, reducing boilerplate constructors.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Unset fields are already the zero value; pointers/flags recover the ability to detect 'unset' when needed.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Good zero-value design is a hallmark of idiomatic, low-friction Go APIs used widely in the standard library.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: http.Server{} is usable at its zero value; you set only Addr and Handler and rely on defaults for the rest.

followUps.question: Give an example where a pointer field is necessary.
followUps.answer: A 'retries' setting where 0 means 'no retries' but you also need to detect 'not configured' — use *int.

followUps.question: How does this reduce boilerplate?
followUps.answer: Callers skip a full constructor and set only non-default fields, since zero values cover the rest.

coding.question: Implement func CelsiusToF(c float64) float64 and explain why type conversions matter here.
coding.thoughtProcess: The formula is c*9/5 + 32. Keep everything float64 to preserve fractions; if c were an int we'd need an explicit conversion to avoid integer division.
coding.lineByLine: c is float64, and the literals 9.0/5.0/32.0 are floats too, so the arithmetic stays floating-point and 37.0 maps to 98.6 rather than being truncated. If c were an int, c*9/5 would do integer division — we'd convert with float64(c) first.

followUps.question: What if the input were an int temperature?
followUps.answer: Convert first: float64(c)*9/5 + 32, otherwise integer division loses precision.

followUps.question: What's the zero-value behavior?
followUps.answer: CelsiusToF(0) returns 32 — a perfectly valid result, no special-casing needed.

coding.question: Implement func SafeRatio(a, b int) float64 that returns a/b as a float64, returning 0 when b is 0. Explain the conversions.
coding.thoughtProcess: Guard b == 0 to avoid an integer divide-by-zero panic and to give a well-defined result (the zero value). For a real ratio, convert both operands to float64 before dividing so the fraction is preserved rather than truncated by integer division.
coding.lineByLine: First we guard b == 0 and return 0, both to avoid the panic integer divide-by-zero would cause and to give a defined result. Otherwise we convert a and b to float64 individually before dividing; doing the conversion first keeps the operation floating-point, so SafeRatio(3, 4) yields 0.75 instead of the 0 that int division would produce.

followUps.question: What happens if you write float64(a / b) instead?
followUps.answer: The int division a/b happens first and truncates, so you'd convert an already-rounded value — the fraction is lost.

followUps.question: Why return 0 rather than panic on b == 0?
followUps.answer: It relies on the zero value as a safe default, keeping callers simple; alternatively you could return an error.

keyTakeaways: Go is statically typed: every variable's type is fixed at compile time.
Declare with var (any scope) or := (inside functions, requires an initializer); := infers the type.
Uninitialized variables get a well-defined zero value: 0, false, "", or nil — never undefined memory.
There are no implicit conversions; convert explicitly with T(x), e.g. float64(i), to avoid bugs like integer division.
